messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 20
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 63

**Patient Vignette: Elias**

Elias is a 20-year-old medical doctor who, by all external measures, has accomplished what few his age could even imagine. He sits at the edge of the chair in my office, his posture rigid, his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He speaks in a low, measured tone, as if he is still in a hospital ward, delivering a prognosis he wishes he did not have to give. He tells me he came because he cannot sleep, and when he does, he wakes up fighting.

Eighteen months ago, Elias was a third-year medical student in his home country, a nation fractured by a sudden and brutal civil conflict. When the front lines shifted, his university was overrun. He was conscripted, not as a soldier, but as the only person with any medical training for miles. He was given a backpack of supplies and told to set up a triage station in a bombed-out school. He was nineteen years old.

He describes the first day as a blur of mud and screaming. He remembers a man, a farmer by the look of his hands, who had been hit by shrapnel in the neck. Elias tried to pack the wound, but the bleeding would not stop. He tells me, his voice flat, that he held the man’s hand as he died. He did not know his name. He says he did that for seven more people that day. He did not stop to eat. He did not stop to cry. He just kept working, because if he stopped, someone else would die.

Now, he is a doctor in a quiet, urban emergency department in a peaceful country. He is grateful for the scholarship that brought him here. But the peace feels like a lie to him. He tells me that every patient who comes in with a cough or a cut feels like a waste of his time. He finds himself getting irritable with the elderly woman who has a sprained ankle, because she is not bleeding. He feels a deep, shameful rage at the mundane nature of his work. The quiet of the ER is the loudest sound he has ever heard.

At night, he does not sleep. He lies in his small apartment, listening for the whistle of a mortar that never comes. He has a strict routine: he checks the locks on his door three times, then the window, then the door again. He keeps a pair of surgical scissors under his pillow. He knows it is irrational, but he tells me he feels “naked” without something sharp nearby.

The worst part, he says, is not the nightmares of the farmer. It is the silence. In the war, the chaos was a signal that he was alive. Now, the silence is a signal that he is waiting. He has not called his mother in three months because he cannot bear to hear her voice. He is terrified that if he hears her cry, he will finally break. He has stopped going to the hospital gym because the sound of the heavy bags being punched sounds too much like the thud of a body hitting the ground.

He looks at me with a hollow clarity. He is not asking for help. He is telling me his history, as if he is presenting a case. He says he came because his hands started shaking yesterday while he was trying to start an IV on a child. He could not do it. He had to ask a nurse to take over. He says he has never failed at anything in his life. He does not know what to do with the feeling of his own hands betraying him. He leaves the session by checking the door handle twice before he opens it.
